article_only_videos.title: Testing Cheap Carbon Handlebars To Failure
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by Berm Peak Express. The presenter says the video is not sponsored by PNW, whose bars he praises; the description promotes his own book, clothing and paid early-access posts. How each tested sample was obtained is not documented.
article_only_videos.summary: A September 2026 home-workshop load test of single samples of low-cost carbon, branded carbon and aluminium handlebars. The presenter separates his static rig from ISO testing; results describe the samples shown, not every bar of a brand or seller.

takeaways.text: The rig pulls both bar ends through a stem with a winch and reads the force on a crane scale. The presenter says it is not an exact ISO procedure and later stresses that it applies a static load, not an impact test.

With one sample of each, the low-cost carbon bars failed at centre loads he read as roughly 600–1,000 lb, mostly between the grip area and the centre. The branded aluminium and carbon reference bars reached his 1,200 lb winch limit without breaking.

A cheap bar printed with a major component brand lacked markings he expected, and he treats it as probably counterfeit; it cracked well below the strongest cheap bars. A familiar logo on a part is not evidence of that brand's testing.

His conclusion is that one result cannot show consistency: repeated testing is what should make every unit fail predictably. New samples also could not show how scratches or impact damage would change the failure point.

takeaways.text: On an older frame with a fixed hanger, he shows how a crash bends it and how repeated straightening can break it. Replaceable hangers became common because they bend or break instead of the frame.
The Transmission derailleur looks frame-mounted, but he explains that it sits where the UDH would be and is held by the thru-axle, so there is no separate hanger left to bend.
He describes UDH as a common hanger that also standardised the frame's rear interface; that shared interface is what lets one direct-mount derailleur fit those frames without a frame-specific hanger.
He calls installation easy once learned but sensitive to tight tolerances: cassette and thru-axle need a torque wrench, which in his words replaces the hanger alignment gauge in the home toolkit.

article_only_videos.title: Proper Use of Torque Wrenches & Drivers: Click Type
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by bicycle-tool maker Park Tool. The demonstration uses its products and the description links to its tools and repair resources. This is manufacturer education, not an independent tool comparison.
article_only_videos.summary: A March 2024 Park Tool demonstration of setting, using and storing its own click-type torque wrenches. It explains technique; torque values come from each component's instructions.

takeaways.text: Setting the wrench means reading the main scale and the fine dial together. On the two models shown, one dial turn adds a different amount, so check your own tool's scale before tightening.

Engage the bit fully and in line with the fastener, pull slowly with your hand centred on the handle, and stop as soon as the head deflects. At low settings the click can be faint, and turning further exceeds the set torque.
Park Tool says these wrenches are length-dependent: holding further back applies less torque than set, choking up applies more, and force should be applied at about 90° to the handle.

For storage, return the setting to the lowest value to unload the spring. Park Tool suggests calibration about yearly or every 5,000–10,000 clicks and warns that dropping the wrench can affect accuracy.

article_only_videos.title: Does Torque Equal Tension? | Tech Tuesday #235
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by bicycle-tool maker Park Tool. The description links to its repair resources and book, credits some footage to a bolting-technology company and links SRAM's recall notice. This is manufacturer education, not an independent test.
article_only_videos.summary: An April 2024 Park Tool explainer on why the same torque can produce different bolt tension when friction changes, with a spoke demonstration. General workshop education, not a torque specification.

takeaways.text: He uses a SRAM shifter-brake clamp bolt recall, linked in the description and involving excess thread-locking compound, as the starting example for why torque alone may not guarantee clamping tension.

Torque is the effort needed to turn the bolt; the useful clamping comes from tension, or preload. Corrosion, damaged threads, oil, grease, water or thread-locking compound change friction, so one torque value can give different tensions.

In his wheel demonstration, spokes brought to the same tension with four different thread preparations showed inconsistent nipple torque; even some spokes with the same preparation differed by more than 300%.
His conclusion: a torque wrench is useful but not a magic wand. Tighten to specification, then verify the joint where possible, for example with a force check.

article_only_videos.summary: An April 2025 Park Tool explainer of headset parts, internally routed designs, external-cup, zero-stack and integrated types, the SHIS headset code and stack height.

takeaways.text: Internally routed cockpits still use the ordinary threadless parts—top cap, stem, spacers, cover and compression ring—but the hoses pass through them, which Park Tool calls tedious to service.

Proprietary headsets exist and industry naming is inconsistent, so Park Tool starts with the bike maker's literature and then uses the SHIS code: fitting type, cup or bearing diameter and steerer diameter.
Stack height is recorded separately. A taller replacement can raise the stem unless spacers are removed, so Park Tool suggests choosing the same or a lower stack height.
In the closing example, the upper and lower bearings get separate codes—here ZS44/28.6 and ZS44/30—each with its own stack height.

article_only_videos.title: Integrated Headset Service - The Easy Way!
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by GCN Tech. The presenter describes a named Park Tool grease in promotional terms, and the description promotes the network's shop, insurance and Zwift club. Whether any product shown was supplied is not stated.
article_only_videos.summary: A September 2026 GCN Tech demonstration of checking and cleaning an integrated headset with internal hoses without disconnecting the brakes, and of when bearing replacement becomes the larger job.

takeaways.text: For a routine check he holds the front brake and rocks the bike, feeling and listening for movement at both bearings, then lifts the front and turns the bars to notice roughness.
Play means either too little preload or worn bearings. He sets preload with the top-cap bolt only as far as needed to remove play, then aligns the bars and tightens the stem bolts to specification.

On this bike the hoses run through the bearings, so he says replacing them means opening the hydraulic system, a bigger job possibly for a shop. His basic service avoids that by lifting the stem within the spare hose length.
Split spacers gave a little extra room, but he notes there was not much spare hose. He wipes surfaces with cleaner on a cloth rather than spraying it at the bearings.

article_only_videos.title: Everything You Need To Know About Power Meters
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by BikeRadar; the description promotes its magazine subscriptions. The presenter names a preferred product and mentions personally owned and previously reviewed units; how each unit shown was obtained is not fully stated.
article_only_videos.summary: An April 2026 BikeRadar explainer comparing crank-arm, spider and pedal power meters and single- versus dual-sided measurement, with the presenter's product preferences.

takeaways.text: A meter bonded to one crank arm ties the build to that crank length. His road unit needed a spacer to suit a gravel chainline, and its smallest chainring was a 34.
A spider meter lets you change crank length, but its chainring mounting limits ring sizes, and the example shown measures both legs without independent left-right balance.
Pedal meters move between bikes because pedal threads are shared, though body type, Q-factor and the cost of replacement bodies still differ by model.
His own dual-sided data put his left-right split at roughly 48/52 to 49/51, and the balance varied more at lower efforts. That is his reason to prefer dual-sided measurement when affordable.

article_only_videos.title: 96% of Cyclists Get Their Tyre Pressure Wrong. How To Get It Right
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by GCN Tech, which says it was given exclusive access to the test facility. The description links an earlier factory video from the premium tyre's maker and promotes the network's shop. The low-cost tyre was bought online; how the premium tyres were obtained is not stated.
article_only_videos.summary: A September 2024 GCN Tech test on a laboratory cycling-efficiency rig, comparing a premium and a low-cost 28 mm tyre across pressures on smooth and cobbled drum surfaces for one rider at one speed.

takeaways.text: The rig measures the efficiency of rider, bike and drum surface as one system while one variable changes and tyre temperature is monitored. It does not isolate a tyre's rolling resistance on its own.

The presenter warns that too little pressure risks pinch flats and sidewall damage. The 28 mm tyres were not bottoming out at 2 bar, but the rig operators said lower would reach the rim, which is why wider tyres permit lower pressure.

On smooth tarmac, both 28 mm tyres with the same TPU tubes were most efficient at 5 bar for this rider at 35 km/h, and the premium tyre stayed more efficient than the cheap one even at a poorer pressure.

On the roughest cobble surface, dropping the premium tyre from 4 to 2 bar cut the measured loss by about 20 W and felt far more comfortable; there, the cheap tyre at 2 bar also beat the premium tyre at 4 bar.

article_only_videos.title: Can You Get Faster With Shorter Cranks?
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by GCN Tech. The presenter thanks the fitting studio for its help, calls one saddle his favourite and discusses buying a particular bike; the description promotes the network's shop, insurance and club. Commercial terms for the session are not stated.
article_only_videos.summary: A May 2026 GCN Tech fitting-jig session in which one presenter tries 165 and 160 mm cranks against his 170 mm baseline and follows the knock-on changes to saddle and handlebar position.

takeaways.text: With only the crank shortened from 170 to 165 mm, motion capture showed his saddle was now too low; the correction is to raise it, not lower it.
Simply adding 5 mm of saddle height also moves the saddle back along the angled seatpost, which closes the hip angle. The jig compensated fore-aft, which in turn changed his reach to the bars.
Keeping the same front end then needed about 5 mm more bar height, which is harder with an integrated cockpit or an already-cut steerer.

With an already comfortable fit, he felt no clear gain at 165 or 160 mm. His conclusion: shorter cranks can help riders who need a more open hip angle, but not everyone needs them, and other changes can open the hip angle too.

article_only_videos.title: How to Size a Bicycle Chain
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by bicycle-tool maker Park Tool. The demonstration uses its products and the description links to its tools and repair resources. This is manufacturer education, not an independent tool comparison.
article_only_videos.summary: A February 2017 Park Tool walk-through of checking an old chain, matching a new chain to it, the largest-sprocket sizing method and the exceptions listed at the time.

takeaways.text: Before copying an old chain, he checks it: in the largest sprockets the shift must still work with a slight bend at each pulley, and in the smallest there should be no slack without the cage pulling the chain onto itself.
When matching a new chain to an old one, line up equivalent plate ends and compare rivet by rivet, remembering that a worn chain has lengthened.
Without a reliable old chain, the common method wraps the chain over the largest ring and largest cog without the derailleur, finds the nearest joinable rivet and adds two more.

The video lists exceptions: route chain guides first, compress rear suspension to its longest chain path, and, at its 2017 publication, SRAM 11- and 12-speed single-ring hardtail systems used four extra rivets instead of two.

article_only_videos.title: DON’T Buy A Used Bike Without Checking THIS
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by GCN Tech. The presenter recommends named Park Tool tools, and the description promotes the network's shop, insurance and club. Whether any product shown was supplied is not stated.
article_only_videos.summary: An August 2026 GCN Tech checklist for inspecting a used bike: wheels and tyres, bearings, drivetrain wear, shifting and hanger, frame and seatpost, brakes, headset and cockpit.

takeaways.text: He spins each wheel to listen for rough bearings, pulls it sideways to feel play, watches the rim for wobble and inspects rims and tyres for damage, cracks on carbon rims and deep cuts.
With the chain lifted off, the cranks should turn smoothly without play. Worn ring and cassette teeth look shark-finned, though shaped shift ramps are normal, and a chain checker shows chain wear.
He inspects high-stress areas such as the bottom bracket, dropouts, brake mounts, seat cluster, clamps and the top tube where a swinging bar can strike, and would walk away from a cracked frame.
He would use a needed brake bleed to negotiate on price rather than walk away, unlike a cracked frame.

article_only_videos.title: Is Your Saddle too far Forward OR Back? (HOW to Set Saddle Fore-Aft)
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by Cam Nicholls. The description links to a paid online bike-fit programme featuring the guest fitter and to the channel's free guide, and the video promotes a paid coaching course. This is the guest's fitting method, not a controlled study.
article_only_videos.summary: An October 2020 interview in which a physiotherapist bike fitter explains signs of a saddle set too far forward or back and a stepwise way to test fore-aft position.

takeaways.text: The fitter dismisses the knee-over-pedal plumb line as a rule because cleat position, limb lengths and knee shape vary between riders.
He compares a bike position to a spider's web: if bar reach or height is far off, set-back cannot be judged in isolation, because changing one contact point moves the others.
Too far forward, he says, tends to load the hands and quadriceps; too far back can strain the hamstrings and stretch the reach, though individual responses vary.
His trial: with the other contact points roughly right, start rearward and move forward in about 5 mm steps with sustained efforts, choosing the most forward position that does not add hand load.

article_only_videos.title: The Fastest Tyre Width is NOT What You Think
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by GCN Tech. The wind-tunnel session ran alongside testing by the wheel brand whose wheels were used, and the description promotes the network's shop, insurance and club. How the tyres and wheels were obtained is not stated.
article_only_videos.summary: A June 2025 GCN Tech test of one road tyre model in 28, 30, 35 and 40 mm for front-wheel aerodynamic drag and rolling losses on smooth surfaces at 30 and 40 km/h.

takeaways.text: He tested one tyre model in four widths with TPU tubes at calculator-recommended pressures, using a wider-rim wheel for the wider tyres; the wind-tunnel part measured a front wheel on its own.
Front-wheel aerodynamic differences were small: about 2.4 W from 28 to 40 mm at 30 km/h, and a 5.1 W penalty for the 40 mm tyre at 40 km/h.
On the efficiency rig the 30 mm tyre lost slightly less power than the 28 mm; the 35 and 40 mm lost more. For a pair, 30 instead of 40 mm saved about 19.5 W at 30 km/h and 24.3 W at 40 km/h.
He expects rougher surfaces to favour wider tyres at lower pressure but did not test that, and says pressure, surface, speed, grip and puncture protection can outweigh width.

article_only_videos.summary: An August 2020 comparison of 1×, 2× and 3× drivetrains by gear steps, range, parts availability, chain life, cost, ease of use and frame design, drawing on the creator's data and third-party tests.

takeaways.text: He compares drivetrains by the cadence drop each shift causes. At his preferred 80–90 rpm, a 1×12 upshift in his example cost about 13 rpm, against about 11 rpm for his 2×11 and 3×10 examples.
With the lowest gear pegged at the same speed, his 1× examples topped out around 47–48 km/h, while the 2× and 3× examples gave roughly 15–20% more top speed.
For beginners he rates 1× the easiest to use and maintain; with two or three rings the rider must also avoid cross-chaining.
Front derailleurs and the inner-ring chainline can interfere with the rear tyre and limit chainstay length, which he gives as a main reason for 1× on mountain bikes.

article_only_videos.title: What Type of Bottom Bracket do I Have?
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by bicycle-tool maker Park Tool. The demonstration uses its products and the description links to its tools and repair resources. This is manufacturer education, not an independent tool comparison.
article_only_videos.summary: A September 2019 Park Tool walk-through for identifying the bottom-bracket type on a bike in hand: press-fit, thread-together and threaded-shell systems.

takeaways.text: With the crank removed, the tool fittings narrow the type: a cup with no external or internal fittings is a press-fit bottom bracket in an unthreaded shell.
Thread-together bottom brackets sit in an unthreaded shell but look much like cups in a threaded shell; Park Tool warns that guessing wrong can damage the frame or components.
Clues include a printed standard such as T47 on the cup or threads visible on only one side inside the shell; if it remains unclear, a cup may need to come out so the shell can be inspected.
The video ends by noting that new standards and tool fittings keep appearing, so the bike maker or a shop may be needed.

article_only_videos.title: How to Align a Hydraulic Disc Brake on a Bike
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by bicycle-tool maker Park Tool. The demonstration uses its products and the description links to its tools and repair resources. This is manufacturer education, not an independent tool comparison.
article_only_videos.summary: A May 2018 Park Tool demonstration of diagnosing hydraulic disc-brake rub and aligning the caliper.

takeaways.text: Diagnosis comes first: with the bike raised and the caliper back-lit, spin the wheel and sight the pad gaps; slight rub with barely any noise may not need adjustment.
Before moving the caliper, check full wheel seating, a bent or loose rotor, hub bearing play and sticking pistons; each can cause or amplify rub.
The basic alignment loosens the caliper bolts, squeezes the lever to centre the caliper, snugs the bolts while holding it and rechecks; finer adjustment moves one bolt at a time.
Add no washers the design did not include. If alignment still fails, Park Tool points to the caliper mounts, which a shop must assess.

article_only_videos.title: How to Convert Your Bicycle Tires to Tubeless
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by bicycle-tool maker Park Tool. The demonstration uses its products and the description links to its tools and repair resources. This is manufacturer education, not an independent tool comparison.
article_only_videos.summary: An August 2016 Park Tool demonstration of converting a wheel to tubeless (rim preparation, tape, valve and troubleshooting) with its stated compatibility limits.

takeaways.text: Park Tool says conversion is possible but limited: ideally both rim and tyre are designated tubeless-ready, yet there is no true industry-wide fit standard, so results vary.
After removing the old rim strip and cleaning the rim channel, choose tape of the right width: too narrow will not seal, and too wide can interfere with the bead seat.
Punch a round valve hole through the tape; in the video, a knife-cut slit is shown as a hole the valve may not cover.
A conversion may take hours or even days to seal, and a non-tubeless tyre in the example seeped air through its sidewalls.

article_only_videos.title: Testing the "EDS" - A Chinese Engineered alternative to Sram AXS

takeaways.text: On his scale the pre-release EDS derailleur and shifter weighed 416 g against 460 g for his SRAM XX1 AXS set.
It did not reach his top gear out of the box; reprogramming needed an app that the manual did not mention, and the app was still marked beta.
On the trail shifting was precise but slower than SRAM AXS when dropping several gears, and the plain thumb buttons felt less refined.
Chain retention over rough ground and a creek crossing caused him no problems, and the battery still showed 75% after the ride.
His main criticism was the user experience, an instruction manual that made little sense in English and an unfinished app, rather than the hardware.

article_only_videos.title: Advanced Bicycle Frame Geometry: Steering Speed, Weight Distribution, Tipping Angles
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by CYCLINGABOUT. The description promotes the channel's own paid buyer's guides and Patreon. The handling figures are calculations from published geometry, including for a bike the creator had not ridden. No sponsor is named.
article_only_videos.summary: An April 2020 CYCLINGABOUT masterclass that uses geometry calculations to show how front centre, chainstay length, trail, luggage and bar width change weight distribution and steering on gravel bikes.

takeaways.text: Longer-reach gravel frames paired with short stems lengthen the front centre: more stability on rough ground and more toe clearance, but some of a seated rider's weight shifts away from the front tyre.

By the creator's calculation, a typical gravel bike carries about 59% of a seated rider's weight on the rear tyre; the long-front-centre example moved a further 0.8–3.3% off the front, depending on size, which matters for grip in flat corners and on steep climbs.
A frame with very long chainstays can reach a similar wheelbase with the extra length behind the rider instead; in smaller sizes it puts more weight on the front tyre. Same total, different split.
Bar and fork luggage adds front load back: the creator estimates roughly 0.8–2 kg on the front would restore a typical gravel bike's front grip, with lighter riders on small frames needing the most.

A longer front centre also enlarges the "endo angle", how far the bike can pitch forward before tipping over the front wheel; the creator names this as the main reason the example should descend steep, rough ground confidently.

Trail, set by head angle and fork offset, is the best single guide to steering speed: less trail steers quicker and helps at low speed, while more trail is calmer at speed but adds wheel flop, which pulls the bars aside on slow climbs.
For slow steering and wheel flop, especially with luggage up front, the creator's first remedy is a wider drop bar for more steering leverage.

article_only_videos.title: How To Fly With An Integrated Cockpit
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by GCN Tech. The presenter praises the named bike box and mini ratchet tool used, and the description promotes the network's shop, insurance and club. Whether those products were supplied is not stated.
article_only_videos.summary: An August 2026 GCN Tech demonstration of packing a road bike with an integrated cockpit for a flight without disconnecting the hydraulic hoses, then reassembling it and checking the headset.

takeaways.text: From more than 15 years of flying with bikes, the presenter prefers a hard case, reporting frame damage only in soft cases, and avoids bars-on boxes because their awkward size and weight complicate transfers and baggage allowances.

Lifting the cockpit off without opening the brakes needs enough spare hose and cable length to lay the bars beside the frame. The presenter suggests trying it well before travel day; if the lines are too short, longer ones and a brake bleed are the fix.
On this bike the stem bolts and top cap came off first, then the bar and stem lifted away, leaving two small wedge clamps; the presenter bags these with the bolts so nothing is lost in the box.
An out-front mount can get in the way, and bolts beneath it can damage the head tube where the bars rest, so the presenter pads between frame and bars and usually removes the mount.
Do not disconnect the hydraulic hoses, which would mean bleeding the brakes at the destination, and avoid kinking them: on reassembly, a kinked hose can leave the lever pulling with no braking.
Reassembly runs in reverse: the top cap goes on first for light bearing preload (this one was marked for a maximum of 2 Nm), then the stem bolts at their recommended torque.

Finally, check for headset play: hold the front brake and rock the bike forwards and back. If the fork moves against the frame, loosen the stem bolts and top cap, press the bars down and set it up again.

article_only_videos.title: How Effective Are Fenders At Keeping Cyclists Clean? | An Ode To Mudguards
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by GCN Tech. One presenter praises the named clip-on mudguards used, and the description promotes the network's shop. Whether they were supplied is not stated. This is an informal visual comparison on one ride, not a measured test.
article_only_videos.summary: A December 2020 GCN Tech demonstration in which two presenters in white suits ride the same muddy loop, one with clip-on mudguards and one without, to show where the spray lands.

takeaways.text: Guards keep a rider clean by stopping the tyres throwing road water up, and a rear guard can also help the rider sitting behind stay cleaner.
For a visual comparison, both presenters wore white suits on the same dirty lanes, one riding with guards and one without.
The clip-on guards used are described as fitting virtually any bike, even one without proper mudguard mounts.
Against guards: the rider without them argues they add weight and drag. For them: they keep the bike and its components cleaner and drier, so parts should last a little longer.
Below the knee both riders looked similar, but the one without guards had a broad stripe of mud up the back.

Their conclusion: the rear guard does most of the work, a front guard mainly keeps feet and lower legs cleaner, and in a group where others ride without guards their spray still reaches you, so the benefit there is slim.

article_only_videos.title: Is Race Geometry DEAD? Specialized Aethos 2 & Factor Monza Change Everything
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by Cycling Weekly. The video contains a paid promotion for a cycling clothing brand, and the description says the publisher may earn commission through affiliate links. How the two test bikes were obtained is not stated.
article_only_videos.summary: A March 2026 Cycling Weekly ride review of two Western road bikes whose geometry is slightly taller and shorter than their brands' race models, comparing fit, weight and ride feel.

takeaways.text: The presenter singles out geometry as the main difference between these bikes and their brands' race models, and as the factor most likely to decide comfort or discomfort on a long ride.

Factor's Monza keeps the Ostro VAM's chainstays, seat angle and head angle but, according to the presenter, is 9 mm taller and 5 mm shorter, so a comfortable position needs fewer stem spacers, which the presenter says would otherwise affect handling.

The Specialized Aethos 2 departs further from the brand's race model: 15 mm taller and 7 mm shorter in reach, with longer chainstays, a 2 mm lower bottom bracket and a half-degree slacker head angle, but the same seat angle, which the presenter thinks shapes how aggressive a bike feels.
The Monza is offered with either a zero-offset or a 25 mm setback seatpost, which the presenter notes is unusual even on race bikes.

On the road, the presenter found the Monza every bit as quick as its race sibling and comfortable enough for daily riding, and the Aethos nimble and very comfortable on long rides, though the presenter was unsure about racing it.
The presenter's conclusion: most riders lack the hip flexibility for the long, low stems professionals use, and both bikes let riders reach a fast but sensible position.

article_only_videos.title: Are Hookless Rims "A Scam"?
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by BikeRadar. It relays one wheel-industry figure's podcast criticism of hookless road rims with responses from wheel brands, and the description promotes the publisher's magazine subscriptions. No sponsor is named.
article_only_videos.summary: A July 2025 BikeRadar explainer on the hookless road-rim debate: ETRTO pressure and tyre-width limits, a prominent critic's safety and aerodynamic claims, and wheel brands' responses.

takeaways.text: Hookless rims lack the bead hooks that traditionally help hold a clincher tyre on under pressure. Brands adopting them cite simpler manufacturing and performance; one major wheel brand kept hooks for what it calls the safest and widest tyre choice.
The worked example: a listener's calculator suggested 76 psi (5.2 bar) at the front, above the 72.5 psi (5 bar) maximum ETRTO sets for hookless rims.
The same 23 mm internal rim width sets a 28 mm minimum tyre under ETRTO and the wheel maker's own rules; the maker confirmed that 25 mm tyres are not compatible with those rims.
The critic says ignoring such limits greatly raises the risk of a tyre blowing off and claims to have seen tyres blow off hookless rims at 78–80 psi.
The wheel maker disputes the aerodynamic criticism: frontal area alone ignores higher yaw angles, grip, comfort and rolling resistance, and it designs around the 28–30 mm tyres riders actually buy.
The critic accepts hookless for gravel and mountain bikes, where tyres are wider and pressures lower, but calls road hookless a scam with no performance advantage.
A leading hookless wheel brand has acknowledged lower production cost but cites lower weight, higher impact resistance and tighter tolerances as further reasons.

After a 2024 race crash, the UCI investigated and reminded teams to follow the latest ISO standards; tyre makers have since added wider sizes to meet rim-width minimums, and the video calls the road debate unsettled.

article_only_videos.title: A Simple Approach to Correct Saddle Height (for road cyclists)
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by Cam Nicholls. The description links to the guest's bike-fitting clinic and to the channel's free e-book and webinar. This is the guest's fitting method, not a controlled study.
article_only_videos.summary: A July 2020 interview in which a physiotherapist bike fitter explains signs of a saddle set too high or too low and a stepwise way to find saddle height on an indoor trainer.

takeaways.text: The fitter says previously fitted riders who arrive with the wrong height are usually too high, and that heights set from some motion-capture knee-angle targets tend to be 10–20 mm too high.

Under a sustained, roughly threshold effort, the fitter looks for smooth, controlled knee extension at the bottom of the stroke; a sudden flick as the leg straightens signals a saddle that is too high.
Burning quads without hamstring fatigue during hard efforts often points to a saddle that is too high, though set-back can also play a part.
With the saddle too high, most riders drop the hip on their dominant side and overextend the other leg; the fitter would rather a saddle be slightly too low than too high.

The trial: heel on the pedal with the leg straight, drop the saddle about 15 mm, then ride sustained efforts on a trainer, raising it 3 mm every 3 minutes until the stroke turns choppy, and go back down 2–3 mm.
Other signs of a well-set height, according to the fitter: less weight on the hands and fatigue spread across quads, hamstrings and glutes rather than one muscle group.

article_only_videos.title: How to Remove and Replace a Derailleur Hanger
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by bicycle-tool maker Park Tool. The demonstration uses its products, and the description links to its tools and to two third-party hanger search sites. This is manufacturer education, not an independent tool comparison.
article_only_videos.summary: A July 2023 Park Tool walk-through of why derailleur hangers bend, how to identify and source the right replacement, and how to install and align it.

takeaways.text: Carbon frames commonly use a replaceable aluminium hanger, but some frames have a hanger that is a permanent part of the frame; both types can be checked with an alignment gauge.
Pedalling puts little stress on the hanger. Bends usually come from impacts such as a crash or knocks in a rack, and repeated bending can lead to failure.
Park Tool suggests buying a spare even for a new bike, because hanger designs have very little interchangeability between brands and models and small differences matter.
To find the right part, note the bike's brand, model and year, take a close-up photo of the hanger, and ask the retailer or manufacturer before turning to hanger databases.
Note how the fasteners sit as the old hanger comes off and keep them if they are in good shape, because replacement hangers do not always include them.
Small M3 hanger screws may take only about 1–1.5 Nm and larger bolts 4–5 Nm; check the frame maker's figure, then check alignment, because frame tolerances can leave even a new hanger out of line.

article_only_videos.title: How we fixed my creaky carbon wheels (Winspace 50mm Hyper)
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by Cam Nicholls; the creator bought the wheels. The work was done at a bike shop linked in the description, which also carries a shortened link to a cycling-clothing brand. This is one shop's fix for one wheelset, not a test.
article_only_videos.summary: A June 2021 visit to a bike shop that traces a creak from the creator's Winspace Hyper 50 rear wheel by reproducing it, servicing several interfaces and opening the freehub.

takeaways.text: The mechanic first reproduced the noise on a ride with the suspect wheels fitted, before changing anything.
The freehub body and cassette interface were greased, and the mechanic pointed to every metal-to-metal contact point, including the thru-axle thread, as a possible creak source.
The mechanic greased the thru-axle thread before tightening it and judged that the axle had never been tight enough before.
A test ride was then quiet; spoke tension measured very high on a tension meter, so the mechanic judged the spokes an unlikely cause.
Opening the freehub showed many pawls with hardly any grease, which the mechanic named as the source of the cracking and called common on wheels straight from the factory.
The pawls were re-greased lightly, checking that each still snapped up under its spring, since too much grease can make them stick.
After 150 km on the wheels, the creator reported no further noise.

article_only_videos.title: Get Your Rotors Tight | Tech Tuesday #215
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by bicycle-tool maker Park Tool. The demonstration uses its products and the description links to its tools and repair resources. This is manufacturer education, not an independent tool comparison.
article_only_videos.summary: An April 2023 Park Tool Tech Tuesday in which a pre-season check traces a braking noise to a loose Center Lock lockring holding a six-bolt rotor adapter.

takeaways.text: During a pre-season check, a noise and extra movement when braking pointed the mechanic to the rear wheel.
The lockring turned by hand: it had simply not been tight. This Center Lock hub carried a six-bolt rotor on an adapter, with the lockring on top.
That lockring's specified torque was 40 Nm. Park Tool's conclusion is that it loosened because it was never properly tightened, not because of how the bike was ridden.
Before final tightening, the mechanic runs the lockring up by hand just short of full effort to learn what the correct torque feels like.

article_only_videos.title: We Stripped, Scanned & Painted a (cheap?) Chinese Carbon Bike
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by Cam Nicholls; the creator bought the frame. The stripping, scanning and repaint were done by a carbon repair and paint shop linked in the description; whether that work was paid for is not stated. This is one shop's assessment of one frame, not a quality report.
article_only_videos.summary: A March 2021 video in which a carbon repair and paint shop strips, inspects and repaints a Winspace road frame the creator bought direct from China, then discusses what it found.

takeaways.text: A carbon repair and paint shop stripped, assessed and repainted a Winspace frame the creator bought direct in 2020; the creator notes the shop does not normally issue end-to-end quality reports.
The process: remove the fittings, measure the decal layout, sand the frame back to inspect it, then paint, add decals, clear-coat and polish.
The specialist, who has seen many Chinese frames, put this one far from the worst examples, such as tubes moulded around stuffed-in catalogues.
The original paint was judged good but not outstanding: a down-tube touch-up had not been polished properly, and the decal was very thick with ragged edges.
Ultrasound found no voids, and thermal imaging, which shows cracks as interruptions in heat flow, was used to look into the layup.
The tube joints were neatly wrapped rather than built up with filler, the seams were tidy, and extra reinforcing layers were visible around the seat tube.
The specialist saw no problem with the manufacturing or layup, but said only the build and ride can show whether the design itself is good.

article_only_videos.title: Externally Vs Internally Routed Cables, Thru-Axle Compatibility & Mullet Bikes | GCN Tech Clinic
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by GCN Tech. A viewer question-and-answer episode; the description promotes the network's shop, insurance and newsletter. No product is reviewed and no sponsor is named.
article_only_videos.summary: An April 2026 GCN Tech viewer Q&A whose last answer covers identifying a replacement thru-axle: markings, length, thread pitch and thread lead, and fitting it gently.

takeaways.text: The presenters say most thru-axles have their dimensions etched on them; otherwise the bike brand's specification list, which can be hard to find, or the same model's axle can identify it.
Length and thread pitch must match, and some brands use a double-lead thread: an axle with the same pitch but a single lead will not thread in the same way.
Fit any new or different-brand axle gently at first; forcing a mismatched axle can strip the dropout threads and potentially ruin the frame.

article_only_videos.title: Do it yourself bicycle service | What you need to know | Cycling Weekly
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by Cycling Weekly. Branded brake pads and a tool maker's chain checker appear in the demonstration, and the description promotes the magazine's riding challenge. No sponsor is named.
article_only_videos.summary: A March 2020 Cycling Weekly home inspection routine for getting a bike ready after winter, working around the bike from wheels and brakes to bearings, contact points and drivetrain wear.

takeaways.text: After a thorough clean, the presenter inspects the bike in an "M" pattern from front wheel to cockpit, bottom bracket, saddle and rear wheel, so no part is skipped.
Tyres are checked for cuts and wear, and tubeless sealant needs checking because it dries out over time.
Hub bearings should spin freely and show no play when the rim is rocked with the wheel clamped in the bike; worn sealed bearings are replaced.
Winter grime is hard on headset bearings, especially the lower one; replacements should match the numbers printed on the old bearings, and tapered headsets use different top and bottom sizes.
A carbon seatpost needs an anti-slip carbon assembly compound rather than ordinary grease, so the clamp can hold it without excessive force.
The chain is measured with a checker rather than judged by eye; the presenter chose to replace a part-worn chain to protect the chainrings and cassette.

article_only_videos.title: 5 Tips For The Perfect Bike Fit
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by CADE Media. The description lists brands that support the channel financially or with products, includes affiliate and discount links, and links to the guest fitter's shop, which sells saddles and shoes discussed in the video. These are one fitter's views, not a controlled study.
article_only_videos.summary: A July 2022 CADE Media video in which a bike fitter summarises common fit problems: handlebar width and reach, saddle height and choice, shoes and cleats, and overall reach.

takeaways.text: The fitter finds handlebars too wide on most bikes: common 52–56 cm frames come with 42 cm bars, while most men measured in the shop are 39–41 cm across the shoulders and most women about 32–38 cm.
The fitter measures across the bony points at the top of the shoulder blades and matches bar width to that, linking bars that are too wide to rolled wrists, numb hands, and neck and shoulder strain.
Bar reach also varies, from about 75 mm to over 100 mm on some stock bars, so the fitter suggests checking it before buying and often prefers a shorter-reach bar.
With the bike level, the fitter sets the drops vertical and the hoods at only a slight slope, so the rider need not roll the wrist to sit on them.
In the fitter's view, excessive reach, along with saddle height, is a main cause of hand, neck, shoulder and saddle problems, with riders compensating by sliding onto the saddle nose.
Reach can come down with a shorter-reach bar, a shorter stem or less saddle setback, though cutting setback too far shifts weight forward.

article_only_videos.title: The Genius of Narrow Wide Chainrings - Why they work!
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by Berm Peak Express. The creator is a part owner of a valve company promoted in the description, which also promotes the channel's Substack and merchandise. The informal test used the channel's own modified bike; no sponsor is named.
article_only_videos.summary: A February 2024 Berm Peak Express explainer on why narrow-wide chainrings hold the chain, with an informal mountain-bike rock-garden test of clutch and chainring combinations.

takeaways.text: SRAM introduced the first narrow-wide mountain-bike chainring in 2012; its teeth alternate between narrow and wide, and many brands followed.
Shimano's 2011 Shadow Plus derailleur added a clutch that puts friction on the cage so the chain moves less over bumps; slow-motion footage shows it still moving, but far less.
In an informal rock-garden test on a modified budget mountain bike, the narrow-wide ring kept the chain on with the clutch on, and even with the clutch switched off.
With a conventional stamped-steel ring, the chain came off almost immediately with the clutch off and still dropped within a 30-second run with it on.
The creator calls the test unscientific and the clutch-versus-ring question a toss-up, but says this test pointed to the narrow-wide ring.
Because the teeth alternate with the chain's inner and outer links, narrow-wide rings come only in even tooth counts, and the chain must sit on the matching teeth when fitted.
A conventional ring's teeth must fit the narrow links, leaving play at the wide ones; filling every gap limits sideways movement and also helps clear dirt.

article_only_videos.title: I Got Winter Cycling Wrong... Here Are My Biggest Mistakes
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by CADE Media. The presenter says none of the product recommendations are sponsored; the description names a channel sponsor and links the channel's Patreon and podcast.
article_only_videos.summary: A January 2026 CADE Media video, filmed in north-east England, on winter riding mistakes: clothing layers, protecting the bike from salt, guards and tyres, route planning and stops.

takeaways.text: Salt from gritted roads sticks to the drivetrain and gets into cables, so riding a summer bike all winter wears its components quickly.
Quoted advice from a hill-climb champion: adapt the bike you have by fitting cheaper, more durable chains, cassettes and chainrings for winter, and worry less about weight or aerodynamics.
Mudguards keep riders dry, which matters because once wet it is hard to get warm; the guards shown include clip-on types for frames without mounts.
To cut stops, the presenters suggest tubeless or puncture-resistant tyres, a frame pump and a bag with tools and spares.
Plan shorter routes closer to home, because wind, cold and ice make everything take longer; one long summer route ended in a rescue call.
Keep café stops short or choose heated ones, eat while riding, and use an indoor trainer when roads are icy.

article_only_videos.title: Custom Bike Build From AliExpress! | Worth The Risk?
article_only_videos.disclosure: Published by GMBN Tech. The parts were bought from an online marketplace for the video; the description carries a discount code for a bike-care brand and promotes the network's shop, insurance and newsletter.
article_only_videos.summary: A January 2025 GMBN Tech attempt to build a full-suspension mountain bike for under £1,000 entirely from marketplace parts, recording delivery, fit, quality and geometry problems.

takeaways.text: Getting every part took three months, with cancelled orders and extra customs paperwork along the way.
The frame arrived without assembly instructions; its rear end was out of alignment, one pivot bearing felt sticky, and paint covered bearing seats that should have been masked or machined.
The coil shock's spring was too large for the frame and hit a pivot; without shock-fit data from the frame maker, the mismatch only showed up during assembly.
The cheap stem arrived with sharp, unfinished machined edges and a clamp so tight it was marked while being fitted.
The presenter judged the cassette in the "groupset" bundle not to be a genuine part of the named brand, as it carried no maker product code.

Several parts did not match: a cassette for the wrong freehub type (an ordering mistake the presenter admits), rotors that never arrived because a listing photo selected another option, and a chainring that would not mesh with the chain.
Measured geometry missed the listing: head angle about 67–68° instead of 65°, seat angle about 72–73° instead of 76°, and a shorter front end than expected for a large.
The presenter's verdict: under £1,000 was reachable on paper, but rework, re-orders and no warranty or support make a discounted brand-name bike the better value.
